subject: VAL
label: Grade 12 Humanities
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 12 Humanities Values and life skills, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 2 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Leadership and ethics
modules.outcome: lead a team project with an ethical review
modules.intro: In this unit, 'Leadership and ethics', you learn to lead a team project with an ethical review. You work with exam-style questions and written reasoning. You see it, say it, then do it alone.
points: Listen and talk: hear a short story, text or example linked to 'Leadership and ethics' and say what it means in your own words.
Connect: name one place in your own day where it applies.
Use it: lead a team project with an ethical review. Practise with care and respect, in class and at home.
Reflect: what went well, what was hard, and one thing you will do next time.
modules.example: Solved: Ethical decision steps: facts, who is affected, options, which value each option meets, choose, review later. Method: Model run for 'Leadership and ethics'. A short text or story is read aloud. Learners say the main lesson in one sentence. In pairs they find one moment in school or home where this lesson would help. Each learner plans one small action for the week and tells it to a partner. At the end of the week they report back. What a good answer looks like: the lesson is in the learner's own words, the example is real and local, and the action is small enough to do. Content follows the approved local syllabus and is checked by a qualified teacher.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Lead a team project with an ethical review: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, The project: Noura leads a team of four on an oral history project about the town's past, interviewing 12 elders. Roles: Noura coordinates, Sami interviews, Dalal transcribes, Faisal designs the booklet.

Step 2, Ethical rules: Get written consent, explain how the stories will be used, quote people accurately, let each person check their quote, and protect anyone who asks to stay anonymous. These five rules guide every interview.

Step 3, Audit consent: After the interviews, Dalal reports that 10 of the 12 gave written consent and 2 agreed only verbally. 10 divided by 12 is about 83 percent. The leader pauses publication until the other 2 are sorted out.

Step 4, Choices: Faisal says, 'Just use all 12, they agreed.' Noura weighs the options: use only the 10, or return and ask the other 2 to sign. Returning respects the elders and keeps all 12 stories, so she chooses it.

Step 5, Accuracy: One elder said, 'We lived near the old well', but the draft says 'We owned the old well.' Noura asks Dalal to fix the quote, because a small change could mislead readers about the family's history.

Step 6, Review the leadership: The 2 elders sign within a week, so all 12 stories are used. The team rates itself out of 5: consent 4, accuracy 5, teamwork 4. Noura notes that she should have asked for signatures at the interview.

Your turn: 9 of 15 survey participants gave written consent. What does the leader do before publishing? Model answer: use only those 9 responses or obtain consent from the other 6, and tell participants how the data will be used.

modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Prepare a study plan, a CV and a statement of purpose: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Study plan: Salma has 10 weeks before exams. She plans 16 hours per week: History 5, Political Science 4, English 4, Sociology 3. Check 5 plus 4 plus 4 plus 3 is 16. Over 10 weeks that is 160 hours.

Step 2, Weekly schedule: History gets two 2-hour sessions and one 1-hour recap; English gets four 1-hour sessions of reading and writing; Sundays are for a past-style question under timed conditions. Fixed times make the plan easier to follow.

Step 3, CV structure: Name and contact, one-line profile, education, achievements, activities and skills. Example bullet: 'Edited the school magazine, publishing 6 issues of 12 pages with a team of 5 writers.' It fits one page.

Step 4, Evidence not adjectives: Instead of 'good writer' she writes 'Wrote 3 articles on local history, read by about 200 students, and interviewed 2 community elders.' Each bullet shows action, size and result, and every number is true.

Step 5, Statement of purpose: Limit 250 words: 40 words opening with the question that drives her, 80 on why history, 80 on evidence from the magazine and oral history work, 50 on goals. 40 plus 80 plus 80 plus 50 is 250.

Step 6, Review: She asks two readers to check clarity and accuracy, makes sure no sentence is copied from a model, and tracks weekly hours, aiming for at least 14 of 16. Honesty and specific detail make an application convincing.
Your turn: Plan 18 hours a week for 4 subjects over 8 weeks. Model answer: for example 6, 4, 4, 4 hours totalling 18; 18 times 8 is 144 hours; include a weekly timed practice.

ladder: L1: kindness, honesty and sharing in daily life.
L2: responsibility, courage and care for others and nature.
L3: fairness, respect for difference and service.
L5: leadership, wellbeing and ethical reasoning.
L6 (degree): applied ethics, culture and community work.
L7 (postgraduate): scholarship, counselling or teaching at depth.
